1) The production of composite vectors by vector boson scattering and Drell-Yan at the LHC is a promising way of testing strong dynamics models with light composite vectors.

the LHC can discover composite vector resonances with a mass of 1 TeV, with the production of the two vector states occurring via the Drell-Yann process.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the phenomenology of composite-vector pairs produced by the Drell–Yan process and by vector-boson fusion at the Large Hadtron Collider (LHC), with particular attention to the case of the minimal left-right gauge model.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
composite-vector pairs at LHC are a very promising signal, but the details of the model, and of the experimental analysis of the signal, are crucial to assess the visibility of such signals.
, if composite-vector pairs are produced at the LHC with rates comparable with those of gauge vectors, their discovery would be possible in a number of different ways.
, in the general case, the composite-vector pair production cross-section is always larger than the one of a gauge-vector pair.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
composite vectors can be produced in a way that resembles the production of the gauge vectors in a SU(2) × SU(2).
the composite vectors are expected to be copiously produced at the LHC and that they may be observed in the multi-lepton channel, provided that the background is under control.
the composite vector scenario, in spite of its generality, is not excluded by the current data from the LHC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LHC can be used to search for a new strong sector even if the only signals are those from composite vectors.
, if the composite vector states are sufficiently light, they may be produced at the LHC in sizable rates, and their discovery would be a clear signature of new physics.
, if a composite-vector pair is discovered with a rate comparable to that of the W pair, then it is unlikely to be the result of a new gauge interaction.
